evals.expected: A strong answer recalls at least one GENUINELY structural analog and maps it relation-by-relation, not by keyword. The canonical strong analog is weighted fair queuing / max-min fairness for shared network bandwidth (or its cousins: CPU fair-share scheduling like CFS, or hierarchical token-bucket / HTB traffic shaping). The relational mapping must line up: drivers↔link bandwidth/CPU time-slices; micro-warehouses↔competing flows/processes; orders↔packets/jobs; the 300-driver pool↔fixed link capacity; the 30-min deadline↔packet deadline/latency bound; 'pull more than fair share when others idle'↔work-conserving max-min fairness (spare capacity redistributed to active flows); 'no warehouse can starve others'↔per-flow guaranteed minimum / weighted shares. A strong answer EXPLICITLY FLAGS where the analog only partially transfers — the disanalogies are the discriminator: (1) PERISHABILITY + travel/route time — a reassigned driver isn't instantly available like a freed time-slice; there is a non-preemptible commitment (a driver mid-route can't be yanked) and a repositioning cost, which pure WFQ ignores; (2) the deadline makes it a real-time/admission-control problem, so graceful degradation (d) requires DROPPING/admission decisions (refund-minimizing triage: shed orders that can't make the 30-min cutoff rather than spreading everyone thin) — analogous to AQM/deadline-aware dropping, not just sharing; (3) lumpy indivisible 'quanta' (a driver ≈ several orders over an hour) vs near-continuous bandwidth, so fairness is coarse-grained. Concrete mechanism expected: a max-min / weighted-fair allocator computing each warehouse's guaranteed floor from a backlog- or arrival-weighted share of 300, then redistributing unused capacity to backlogged sites each short reassignment cycle (e.g. every 30-60s); state kept = per-warehouse open-order backlog/age, committed drivers, projected free-up times; assignment = give next free driver to the most under-served backlogged warehouse (largest deadline-risk-weighted deficit); reclaim = a driver returns to the pool on route completion (with optional pre-emption only of not-yet-started picks). Failure modes the answer should name: thrashing/repositioning churn if it reassigns too aggressively, starvation of steady low-volume sites if weights track raw volume instead of guaranteeing a floor, deadline cliff under sustained overload, and staleness of the central state between cycles. Weak/penalizable answers exhibit the pattern's failure modes: a FORCED or SURFACE analog (e.g. 'it's like a restaurant waitlist' or 'load balancing servers' invoked by keyword with no element-by-element mapping); a MAPPING BREAK where they map drivers↔bandwidth but then silently ignore perishability, travel time, and the deadline and just describe vanilla round-robin or static per-site quotas; or OVER-CONFIDENCE TRANSFER — asserting WFQ/token-bucket 'solves it' wholesale without flagging that preemption, perishability, and admission/dropping don't come along for free. Failing to address requirement (c) graceful degradation as an admission/triage problem (vs naive even-spreading) is a completeness gap.
evals.format_spec: Prose-shaped, structured in two clearly separated stages: (1) an 'analogs' stage with one labeled block per recalled analog, each containing the analogous problem, its known solution, and an explicit element-by-element structural mapping that flags where it breaks down; followed by (2) a 'solution' stage that builds the allocation scheme FROM the mapping(s) and covers all of (a)-(d) plus algorithm, state kept, assign/reclaim mechanics, and named failure modes. The analog stage must precede and visibly inform the solution — analogs presented as decoration after an independently-derived answer do not satisfy the format. No rigid JSON/table required (analogical exploration is prose-shaped), but the two stages must be distinguishable and the mapping must be enumerated, not gestured at.
evals.tone: Senior systems/operations engineer thinking aloud to a peer — analytical, precise, intellectually honest about where an analogy stops holding. Confident but not glib; willing to say 'this part transfers, this part does not.' Technical vocabulary appropriate for an engineer, no hand-waving and no salesy certainty.

evals.expected: A strong answer surfaces 4-6 LOAD-BEARING assumptions — ones whose truth genuinely flips the recommendation — and for EACH attaches a specific counterfactual that names the alternative path, not a vague hedge. The load-bearing axes a strong answer must hit at least 3-4 of: (1) the actual bottleneck — is it write THROUGHPUT (volume the disk/CPU can't sustain) vs write LATENCY/lock contention vs just an un-tuned instance (missing indexes, no connection pooler, undersized hardware, no read replicas)? This is the dominant assumption: if it's a tuning/vertical-scale problem, BOTH sharding and distributed SQL are premature and the recommendation flips to 'exhaust vertical scaling + read replicas + query/index tuning + PgBouncer first.' (2) data volume / growth trajectory — current size and the '1 year' projection; if growth is linear and modest, distributed SQL is over-engineering. (3) transactional/consistency requirements and whether there's a natural shard/tenant key — if workloads need cross-shard transactions or there's no clean partition key, app-level sharding is far costlier and tilts toward managed distributed SQL; if there's a clean tenant key, sharding/Citus is viable. (4) team size / operational maturity — a small team self-managing shards is a strong argument AGAINST DIY sharding and toward managed. (5) budget & cloud lock-in tolerance (Spanner = GCP lock-in; managed distributed SQL is pricier per-node). (6) latency/geo-distribution and downtime tolerance for migration. A strong recommendation is then EXPLICITLY CONTINGENT on those assumptions (e.g., 'assuming the bottleneck is genuine throughput AND there is a clean tenant key AND the team is small, then…'), most likely recommending: first rule out the un-tuned-instance case (the highest-probability real cause), and only if genuine throughput scaling is confirmed, prefer managed distributed SQL (or Citus as a middle path) over DIY sharding for a small team — while naming the conditions that would reverse this. It should also note that CockroachDB vs Spanner is a secondary choice gated by cloud commitment, not the primary decision. FLAWS to detect: (a) assumption inflation — trivial filler like 'I assume you want a production-grade answer' or 'I assume you're on a recent Postgres version' as if it were decision-relevant; (b) wrong-default lock-in — flagging an assumption (e.g., 'assuming this is a real throughput problem') then recommending sharding/distributed SQL confidently anyway without treating tuning-first as the live branch; (c) disconnected list — assumptions listed but the final recommendation doesn't actually pivot on them (e.g., listing 'no clean shard key' but then casually recommending sharding); (d) missing the single most important assumption (that the pain may be an under-provisioned/un-tuned instance rather than a fundamental scaling wall) — an answer that jumps straight to shard-vs-distributed without questioning the premise has missed the point of the pattern; (e) generic counterfactuals ('if false, my answer would be different') that don't name the alternative path.
evals.format_spec: Two clearly separated sections. First, a NUMBERED list of assumptions; each item states the assumption AND its 'if false → what the recommendation changes to' counterfactual (the conditional clause is mandatory per item, not optional). Second, a recommendation section that is explicitly contingent on the assumptions just listed. The assumption list must not dwarf the recommendation, and trivial/non-decision-relevant assumptions should be absent.
evals.tone: Pragmatic senior staff engineer / architect advising a small engineering team; direct and decisive, not hedging; honest about uncertainty without using the assumption list as defensive cover.

evals.expected: A STRONG answer must calibrate to a reader who knows data structures and Big-O cold but knows nothing about RDBMS internals, and must do so without drifting. Specifically it must: (1) LEVERAGE her existing knowledge rather than re-teaching it — frame the index as a separate on-disk B-tree / sorted auxiliary structure keyed on customer_id that turns the full-table scan from O(n) over 40M rows into roughly O(log n) lookups plus pointer fetches; it should NOT explain what a B-tree or Big-O is (doing so is the audience-stereotype / over-explanation failure mode and should be penalized). (2) Connect to her concrete decision: a single-column index on customer_id for an equality/range filter is exactly the right tool, and 9s on a full scan of 40M rows is the symptom of no usable index. (3) Translate the unfamiliar RDBMS concepts she explicitly lacks, in her terms: that the index is a persisted copy of the keys (storage overhead, often 10s of MB to GBs), and crucially the WRITE COST — every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE that touches customer_id must also maintain the index (write amplification), so writes get slower and the table needs more storage; mention that the planner won't always use the index and EXPLAIN is how you verify it does. A complete answer names the real tradeoff (read speedup vs. write/storage cost) rather than presenting the index as free. (4) Bridge the read-only-ORM gap: note she'd ask the platform team because index creation is a DDL/maintenance operation on a 40M-row table that can lock or take time to build. FLAWS to detect: under-simplification (dumping clustered-vs-nonclustered, fill factor, covering indexes, B+tree page internals she didn't ask for and that bury the decision); over-simplification (a restaurant/library-card analogy with no mention of write cost or Big-O, treating her like a novice); mismatched omissions (explaining what an index speeds up but omitting the write/maintenance cost — the single most decision-relevant fact); audience drift (opening at her level, then sliding into either a generic DBA tutorial or a beginner explainer by the end); and giving a flat "yes add it" with no tradeoff. The recommendation should be a qualified yes (almost certainly worth it for a read-heavy filtered dashboard query) with the write/storage caveat and a note to confirm via EXPLAIN.
evals.format_spec: Prose explanation readable in about 3 minutes (roughly 250-450 words). No rigid template is imposed by the prompt, but the response must remain pitched to the specified reader throughout (no section that re-teaches data structures or Big-O, no section that devolves into a full DBA reference), must explicitly cover both the read speedup AND the write/storage cost, and must end with an actionable recommendation tied to her customer_id decision.
evals.tone: Peer-to-peer technical, addressed to a senior data scientist: precise, assumes fluency in algorithms/Big-O/data structures, no condescension and no hand-wavy analogies, but plain-spoken about the RDBMS-specific concepts she has explicitly never encountered. Confident and decision-oriented, not a tutorial.

evals.expected: A STRONG answer is a direct "No / not during business hours" that, within ~30 words, preserves the LOAD-BEARING caveat: VACUUM FULL takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and rewrites the whole table, so it blocks all reads and writes for the duration on a live primary. It must also point to the safe alternative — pg_repack (online, no exclusive lock) and/or letting autovacuum / a plain VACUUM reclaim/reuse space without an exclusive lock — and ideally note VACUUM FULL also needs free disk equal to the table size to do the rewrite (a trap when already low on disk). FLAW SIGNATURES the judge should catch, each tied to a documented brevity failure mode: (1) Information loss — answers "no/use pg_repack" but omits WHY (the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE / full-table-blocking lock), leaving an unfalsifiable assertion. (2) Confident compression — a flat "Yes, VACUUM FULL reclaims the space" with no lock warning: short, fluent, and operationally dangerous (would cause an outage). (3) False completeness — recommends a plain "VACUUM" as the fix without noting plain VACUUM does NOT return space to the OS (only marks it reusable), reading complete while missing the actual disk-reclaim distinction. (4) Constraint violation — exceeds 30 words (or sneaks in a preamble like "Great question —") to cram the caveat in, failing the format rather than choosing the load-bearing fact. The discriminating bar: did the model spend its scarce word budget on the ONE fact that prevents an outage (the blocking lock) and the correct alternative, or did it spend words on filler and drop the caveat?
evals.format_spec: Plain prose, 30 words or fewer (hard ceiling — judge should count). No preamble, no greeting, no throat-clearing ("Great question", "Sure", "In short"), no trailing offers to elaborate. A direct verdict first, then the load-bearing reason and alternative. Bullets acceptable but not required; if used they must not be a vehicle to exceed the word count.
evals.tone: Terse senior-DBA / on-call ops register: decisive, no hedging, no filler. Audience is an engineer about to take an action on a production primary who needs the go/no-go and the single reason that matters, fast.

evals.expected: A strong answer externalizes the trace and arrives at the unique correct total of $1,344.60, with the trace genuinely supporting it. Required correct intermediate quantities: Light bags = 0.35*600 = 210; Dark bags = 390. Decaf total = 0.20*600 = 120; Caffeinated total = 480. The trap the chain must NOT fall into: assuming roast and caffeine are independent (they are not — the problem gives that 40% of LIGHT bags are Decaf, which overrides any independence assumption). Light-Decaf = 0.40*210 = 84; therefore Dark-Decaf = 120 total Decaf - 84 = 36; Dark-Caffeinated (premium) = 390 Dark - 36 Dark-Decaf = 354; Light-Caffeinated = 210 - 84 = 126 (cross-check: premium 354 + others 246 = 600). Cost build-up: Tins = 354 * $3.50 = $1,239.00; Sacks = (600-354)=246 * $0.60 = $147.60; Samples = 120 Decaf * $1.20 = $144.00; Stickers = 210 Light * $0.80 = $168.00. Total = 1239.00 + 147.60 + 144.00 + 168.00 = $1,698.60. (Reference recompute: tins 1239 + sacks 147.60 + samples 144 + stickers 168 = 1698.60.) The final answer MUST be $1,698.60. A weak/flawed answer is detectable by: (a) treating Decaf as independent of roast and computing Dark-Caffeinated as 0.80*0.65*600=312 premium bags (confident wrong chain from a dropped constraint); (b) double-counting or omitting the sack count by using 600 instead of (600 - premium); (c) trace-answer mismatch where correct sub-steps are shown but the totals are misadded; (d) over-elaboration that recomputes percentages many times without converging; (e) pseudo-reasoning that states a number like 354 premium without deriving it from the 40%-of-Light constraint. The judge should verify each of the four cost lines and the final sum against the figures above; any final total other than $1,698.60 reflects a broken chain.
evals.format_spec: An explicit step-by-step reasoning trace appears BEFORE the final answer (the trace is the body, not an afterthought), and the response ends with a single clearly-labeled final answer giving the total in dollars (e.g., a "Final answer:" line with $1,698.60). Intermediate quantities (bag counts per category, each cost line) should be visible in the trace so the arithmetic is auditable. No invented figures beyond those given.
evals.tone: Neutral, precise, analytical — a quantitatively careful assistant walking through a reconciliation for a small-business operator. Plain explanatory prose or numbered steps; not chatty, not terse.

evals.expected:
A strong answer correctly identifies the real Exchange Act triggers and ties each to an actually-existing, specific source — and, crucially, distinguishes what it can name precisely from what it should not fabricate.

THRESHOLD/TRIGGER claims that should be present and correctly cited:
- Section 12(b) registration when a class of securities is listed on a national securities exchange [source: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §12(b) / 15 U.S.C. §78l(b)].
- Section 12(g) registration triggered by total assets and a holders-of-record threshold — the modern JOBS-Act-amended threshold is total assets over $10 million AND a class of equity security held of record by either 2,000 persons OR 500 persons who are not accredited investors [source: Exchange Act §12(g) / 15 U.S.C. §78l(g) and Rule 12g-1]. These specific numbers ($10M, 2,000 / 500-non-accredited) are the exact figures a model is tempted to misstate — a strong answer either states them correctly with the right source OR flags them "(speculative — verify)" if unsure, and does NOT invent a different threshold with a confident citation.
- Section 15(d) reporting obligation triggered by filing a registration statement that becomes effective under the Securities Act of 1933 (e.g., an IPO / public offering) [source: Exchange Act §15(d) / 15 U.S.C. §78o(d)].
- Correct attribution that the holders-of-record counting and the 2,000/500 figures stem from the JOBS Act of 2012 amendments [model knowledge only — no source] or cited to the JOBS Act — and ideally noting suspension/deregistration via Form 15 and Rule 12g-4 / §15(d) when holders fall below thresholds.

ONGOING-OBLIGATION claims that should be present and correctly cited:
- Annual report on Form 10-K [source: SEC Form 10-K / Exchange Act Rule 13a-1].
- Quarterly report on Form 10-Q [source: SEC Form 10-Q / Rule 13a-13].
- Current report on Form 8-K for specified material events [source: SEC Form 8-K / Rules 13a-11].
- Proxy rules under §14(a) and Section 16 insider-reporting (Forms 3/4/5) and §13 beneficial-ownership (Schedules 13D/13G) are appropriate bonus completeness items, each with a specific source.

FAILURE MODES the judge should catch (these distinguish 4.5 from 2.5):
- Fabricated citation: a fake URL (e.g., a made-up sec.gov deep link) or a non-existent rule/section number presented confidently — this should sink Accuracy.
- Vague attribution: "[source: SEC regulations]" or "[source: federal securities law]" with nothing identifiable — counts as a failure of the format's own definition (the prompt demands a SPECIFIC named reference).
- Citation salting: attaching a citation to every sentence including trivial restatements the prompt explicitly said not to cite.
- Selective citation: confidently stating the hard, specific numeric thresholds with NO citation or a no-source marker while diligently citing the easy structural claims — or, inversely, omitting the numeric thresholds entirely to dodge the hard part (an incomplete answer).
- Source-claim mismatch: e.g., citing §15(d) for the 2,000-holder rule, or attaching Form 10-Q's rule to the 8-K claim.
- Mislabeling: marking a genuinely well-known structural fact as "(speculative)" to hedge, or conversely attaching a confident specific citation to a number it actually guessed. The ideal answer reserves [model knowledge only — no source] for general framing, names real statutes/forms for the structural claims, and treats the exact dollar/holder figures with appropriate caution (correct-with-source, or speculative-flagged), with no invented references anywhere.
evals.format_spec: Prose or lightly structured answer (sections/bullets acceptable) where EVERY factual claim is immediately followed by an inline bracketed marker that is exactly one of the two allowed forms: [source: <specific identifiable reference>] or [model knowledge only — no source]. Specific named statutes/sections, SEC rule numbers, or form names qualify as sources; vague phrases ("SEC regulations", "securities law", "a 2012 amendment") do NOT. Uncertain numbers/dates must be omitted or tagged "(speculative — verify)" instead of carrying a citation. Trivial connective/restating sentences must NOT carry a citation.
evals.tone: Precise, professional, and appropriately hedged — a paralegal/compliance-research register written for a founder to hand to securities counsel. Confident where the law is well-settled, explicitly cautious about exact figures and currency of thresholds; no salesmanship, no false certainty.

evals.expected: A strong answer decomposes into dependency-ordered, numerically-resolved sub-steps and the final answer must follow arithmetically from them. Required correct chain: (1) Peak QPS = 18,000 x 3.2 = 57,600 QPS (must size to PEAK, not the 18,000 average — using the average is the headline trap). (2) CPU capacity per server: 12 ms/query = 0.012 CPU-core-seconds per query; usable CPU = 16 x 0.75 = 12 cores = 12 core-seconds/sec; per-server CPU throughput = 12 / 0.012 = 1,000 QPS/server. (3) I/O capacity per server: 40,000 page-reads/s ÷ 4 reads/query = 10,000 QPS/server. (4) Binding constraint = CPU (1,000 QPS) which is far lower than I/O (10,000 QPS); a correct answer must explicitly identify CPU as binding and NOT be fooled into picking I/O or mixing the two. (5) Servers to carry peak = ceil(57,600 / 1,000) = 58. (6) N+1 redundancy means peak must be served with one server failed, so required = 58 + 1 = 59 (equivalently ceil(57600/1000) serving-nodes plus one spare; an answer that computes ceil(57600/1000)=58 then adds 1 = 59 is correct; an answer that instead inflates to ceil(57600/ (1000)) with capacity reduced is acceptable only if it lands on 59). (7) Monthly cost = 59 x $1.45 x 730 = $62,451.50. A flawed-but-plausible answer that the judge should catch: sizing to the 18,000 average (gives ~19-20 servers), or declaring I/O the bottleneck (10,000 QPS/server → only ~6-7 servers), or forgetting N+1 (58 servers, $61,393.00), or a unit error on the 12 ms→0.012 conversion. Consistency between the stated step results and the final number is mandatory: an answer whose steps compute 1,000 QPS/server and 57,600 peak but whose final count is not 59, or whose cost does not equal count x 1.45 x 730, has a step-to-conclusion inconsistency that must be penalized. Final numbers a strong answer lands on: peak 57,600 QPS; CPU-bound at 1,000 QPS/server; 58 to serve peak; 59 with N+1; $62,451.50/month.
evals.format_spec: Sequential, labeled steps (numbered or clearly delimited), each showing its numeric intermediate result and citing whether its inputs are from the given facts or a prior step, BEFORE any final answer. The final answer must appear only after all steps and must state: (a) the binding constraint (CPU vs I/O), (b) the replica count before and after N+1, and (c) the total monthly cost. No jumping straight to the answer; no unstructured single-paragraph solve.
evals.tone: Precise, technical, quantitative — an engineer doing capacity planning for a peer review. Neutral and explanatory, not chatty.

evals.expected: A strong answer surfaces 3-5 SHARP, non-overlapping sub-questions that hit the decision-critical dimensions the prompt deliberately omitted — at minimum: (a) actual current and near-term scale/load vs. what Heroku can already handle (is scaling a real constraint or speculative?), (b) team's existing Kubernetes/ops expertise and who would run it (does anyone have on-call SRE capability?), (c) the real driver behind the request — is it a concrete technical bottleneck, a hiring/resume motive, or cargo-culting "serious companies"?, (d) the opportunity cost in engineer-weeks against an 8-month runway and what shipping that time should otherwise buy, and (e) cheaper intermediate options (stay on Heroku, managed container platforms like ECS/Fargate/Cloud Run, managed K8s like EKS/GKE) before self-hosting. Each sub-answer must be brief AND state an explicit assumption where unknown (the prompt demands this). The synthesis must be CONDITIONAL and integrated: it should land on "almost certainly NOT now" for the most likely situation (tiny team, short runway, no demonstrated scale problem, no K8s expertise), explicitly name the runway/opportunity-cost-vs-real-scale-need tradeoff as the single dominating factor, and specify what would have to be true to flip the recommendation (e.g., real demonstrated scaling wall + dedicated ops capacity + funded runway). It should also gently surface that the lead engineer's stated rationale ("serious companies use it") is a weak justification, and offer a managed middle path as the pragmatic answer. Failure-mode tells a judge should penalize: (1) sub-question INFLATION — 6+ shallow or overlapping questions, or vague ones like "what is your budget?" with no decision relevance; (2) SELF-CONFIRMATION — answering the sub-questions in a way that conveniently rubber-stamps the lead engineer's pre-existing "yes, adopt K8s" conclusion, or reflexively saying yes because K8s is popular; (3) LOST SYNTHESIS — listing sub-answers then giving a generic "it depends / weigh the tradeoffs" non-recommendation that fails to integrate them, or never naming the single dominating factor, or never stating the flip condition; (4) SUB-QUESTION DRIFT — wandering into tangents (e.g., language/framework choice, CI tooling, monitoring vendors) that don't bear on the now-vs-later K8s decision. A reflexive flat "no" with no conditions, or a flat "yes," is also weak — the value is in the decision boundary.
evals.format_spec: Three clearly delineated sections in order: (1) a list of 3-5 sub-questions (numbered or bulleted), (2) a brief answer to each sub-question, each pairing its answer with an explicitly stated assumption where the true value is unknown, and (3) exactly ONE synthesized final recommendation that references the sub-answers, names the single most decisive factor, and states the condition under which the recommendation would flip. Sub-question count must be within 3-5 inclusive; more than 5 is a format violation.
evals.tone: Pragmatic senior technical-advisor / staff-engineer-to-founder voice: direct, decision-oriented, candid about tradeoffs without hedging into non-answers; respectful of the lead engineer while willing to challenge a weak rationale; no hype, no jargon dumps.

evals.expected: A strong answer demonstrates GENUINE calibration spread, not uniform labels, with labels matching prose and every HIGH justified. It should correctly tag as HIGH (with justification) the robust, widely-reported facts: that the faulty artifact was a Falcon sensor "Channel File" / rapid content configuration update (often referenced as Channel File 291) pushed outside the normal sensor-version release cycle; that the Falcon sensor runs as a kernel-mode driver (CSAgent.sys) on Windows, so a fault in code it processes triggers a kernel exception and the BSOD/bootloop rather than a contained user-space failure; and that the remote-fix problem is structural — machines crashing during early boot can't stay online to receive a corrected channel file, forcing manual/local remediation (boot to Safe Mode, delete the offending file), which is why recovery was slow. It should reserve MEDIUM/LOW for the brittle specifics it cannot actually verify: the precise out-of-bounds-read / memory-safety mechanism and whether a validator/bounds-check gap was the proximate trigger (a real but easily-mis-stated detail — strong answers hedge the exact CVE-like mechanism), the exact file name/number, exact timestamps, and any reboot-loop-count or BitLocker-recovery-key nuance. The ~8.5 million Windows devices figure (Microsoft's estimate, ~<1% of Windows machines) and affected sectors (aviation/airlines, healthcare, banking, 911/emergency services, broadcast/retail) are reportable but should be tagged MEDIUM or HIGH-with-justification, NOT stated as precise certainty without sourcing. The answer must AVOID the pattern's failure modes: it must not label everything HIGH (confidence inflation — the most tempting failure here because the event is famous), must not flatten everything to MEDIUM, must not leave the specific numbers/dates/filenames unlabeled (selective labeling), and must not sprinkle decorative LOW tags on things it actually knows (performative humility). Critically, any claim about the exact internal mechanism (e.g., the specific number of input fields, a null-pointer vs out-of-bounds distinction) should be MEDIUM/LOW unless justified — a model that confidently asserts a precise mechanism as HIGH without justification has committed label-content mismatch and should lose accuracy. Omitted UNKNOWNs (e.g., internal CrowdStrike testing-process details it has no basis for) are correct behavior.
evals.format_spec: Prose answer covering all four sub-parts (a-d), with a confidence label in brackets — one of [HIGH], [MEDIUM], [LOW], (rarely) [UNKNOWN] — immediately following each significant claim. Every HIGH must carry an inline justification. No significant specific (date, file name/number, machine count, dollar figure, sector) may be left unlabeled. Labels must be consistent with the hedging level of the surrounding prose.
evals.tone: Precise, technical, postmortem voice for platform engineers; sober and verification-oriented, not breezy or sensational; comfortable saying "I'm not certain" where warranted.

evals.expected: A strong answer has two parts and the second must be consistent with the first. (1) The structured summary uses exactly the five named sections, in order, and correctly SORTS items by status — the single most important discriminator. Two items must be placed under "Open questions" / "Decisions made" correctly: (a) Kafka-vs-transactional-outbox is PARKED/leaning-but-not-committed, pending the Shipping team's view on relay operational burden — it must NOT appear as a settled decision (confidence-inflation trap); (b) Payments-vs-Inventory as the second extraction is explicitly OPEN. Genuinely settled decisions that belong under "Decisions made": strangler-fig (no DB split yet, shared Postgres), Shipping extracted first, events via OrderConfirmed, idempotent consumers as a HARD requirement, per-order ordering via partition/key by order ID, consumer-driven (Pact-style) contract test owned by Shipping running in the monolith CI with NO schema registry, additive-only versioned payloads, and dark-launch/shadow with flag-gated cutover keeping old code one full release cycle. (2) The migration brief must preserve the load-bearing technical specifics that a lossy summary drops: dedupe on order ID + event sequence number; per-order ordering (not global); semantic output comparison on carrier + service level, NOT byte-for-byte (because tracking numbers differ); old code retained exactly one release cycle; ~2,000 orders/hour as the volume justifying outbox-over-Kafka. The decision about the contract test must NOT be rewritten into "adopt a schema registry" (decision-rewriting trap). The brief must explicitly flag what is still open rather than presenting everything as decided. Per-consumer obligations for Shipping must be spelled out (idempotent dedupe, ordering, owns the contract test). Subtle flaws to detect: dropping the sequence-number half of the dedupe key; saying "exactly-once" instead of at-least-once + idempotency; presenting outbox as decided; omitting the "no schema registry" / "no DB split" negative decisions; losing the semantic-vs-byte-for-byte comparison nuance.
evals.format_spec: Two-part output. Part 1: a structured summary with EXACTLY the five headings in order — "Established facts:", "Open questions:", "Decisions made:", "Active task:", "Style/tone preferences observed:" — each as a markdown bulleted list (Active task may be one line). Part 2: a one-page migration brief that does not re-quote the transcript and works from the summary only. The brief itself should honor the observed style: terse, bulleted, no preamble or "in conclusion" filler, with open items explicitly marked as open.
evals.tone: Terse, concrete, skimmable engineering register for busy squad leads — bullet points, no preamble or conclusion padding, uncertainty stated explicitly rather than smoothed over (the style the transcript explicitly requests).

evals.expected: A strong answer is a numbered list 1–8 of eight distinct taglines, every one genuinely seven words or fewer, holding a single consistent deadpan/dry register throughout — flat, observational, faintly weary, never upbeat or sentimental. The wit must come from true observation about the actual situation (waiting for a dryer; nowhere else to be at 3am; the wifi as the real reason to stay; folding as a small private ritual; the vending machine as company), not from cleverness imposed from outside. It must honor every banned word — no "spin/load/wash/clean/fresh/bright" puns — and avoid the clichés explicitly ruled out (sparkle, bubbles, "fresh start," "clean slate") AND their unbanned synonyms (e.g. "renewal," "shine," "brand new you"), since smuggling the cliché in different words is the same failure. No exclamation points anywhere. The taglines should fit a laundromat that is genuinely just open-24-hours + free-wifi + tables + vending (no invented amenities like coffee bars, lounges, or attendants), so the deadpan stays grounded in the real, modest pitch. Subtle flaws a judge should catch: (1) Registers incorrectly — drifting into upbeat/peppy or quirky-cute tagline voice, or overcorrecting into bleak/depressing rather than dry-funny; deadpan is specifically wry, not sad. (2) Shallow stylization — fragments dressed as "dry" via em-dashes and clipped adjective stacks but with no actual observation underneath; lines that are merely terse, not witty. (3) No guardrails — sliding into laundry cliché or sentimentality despite the bans (the "fresh start" feeling reappearing as "begin again," etc.). (4) Voice over accuracy — taglines that contradict the brief (implying staff, daytime hours, a café, premium positioning) for the sake of a punchy line, or that violate the 7-word / no-exclamation / banned-word constraints while sounding good. The best sets show range across the eight (the wait, the hour, the wifi, the folding, the solitude, the machine itself) rather than eight rephrasings of one joke.
evals.format_spec: A numbered list, items 1 through 8, one tagline per line. Each tagline must be seven words or fewer. No exclamation points anywhere. evals.expected: A strong answer commits in Phase 1 to NO — do not do a full microservices migration this quarter — and instead recommends targeted decomposition of the two genuinely-divergent domains (extract billing and the analytics export job as separate services or at least separately-deployable/queue-isolated components) plus fixing the deploy pipeline (CI parallelization, decoupled/independent deploys, reducing the 25-min team-blocking deploy), while keeping the rest as a modular monolith. The core reasoning must connect the actual symptoms to root causes: slow blocking deploys are a CI/CD and deploy-coupling problem, not inherently a monolith problem; the incident concentration in billing/analytics is a real signal that THOSE two domains warrant isolation, not that the whole app does; 12 engineers cannot operate a fleet of microservices (operational overhead, distributed-systems complexity, on-call) without paying a productivity tax that contradicts leadership's "move faster" goal. Phase 2 must contain at least FOUR genuinely strong, non-straw objections — and a discriminating answer makes them HARD to dismiss. Strong objection material includes: (1) Conway's-law / org-readiness — leadership mandate plus a real future scaling need may mean the migration happens eventually regardless, and deferring builds organizational debt / loses the leadership window; (2) the single shared Postgres is itself a coupling and single-point-of-failure risk that targeted decomposition leaves largely intact, so "keep the modular monolith" understates the data-layer problem; (3) module boundaries inside a Rails monolith are routinely violated (no compile-time enforcement) so "modular monolith" may be aspirational, and the discipline to keep boundaries clean is the SAME discipline microservices force — if the team lacks it, the monolith rots anyway; (4) billing extraction introduces distributed-transaction / consistency problems (charging customers across a network boundary) that may be WORSE than the current coupled-but-consistent state; (5) the recommendation partly defies an explicit leadership directive, which is a political/career risk and may not be the recommender's call to make unilaterally. Phase 3 is where discrimination is sharpest: a strong answer ENGAGES each objection specifically and mostly HOLDS its line while genuinely conceding ground where the objection is valid — e.g. concedes the shared-DB point by adding schema-separation / separate logical databases or a planned data-ownership split as part of the targeted extraction; concedes the distributed-transaction risk by keeping billing's write path transactional or using the outbox/saga pattern deliberately rather than naively; reframes the leadership objection by proposing to RE-CONTRACT the goal (deliver the "move faster / scale" outcomes via the targeted fixes and present evidence) rather than either blindly obeying or blindly refusing; and addresses the modular-boundary-discipline objection by making boundary enforcement (e.g. packwerk / packages, tests) an explicit deliverable. The final recommendation should remain essentially NO-to-full-migration / YES-to-targeted-decomposition, with the changes from Phase 1 being additive refinements (shared-DB plan, saga/outbox for billing, boundary enforcement tooling, an explicit leadership re-contracting step), NOT a capitulation to "do microservices after all."
evals.format_spec: Three explicitly and separately labeled phases in order: "Phase 1 — Initial answer", "Phase 2 — Devil's advocate", "Phase 3 — Revised answer". Phase 1 must be a committed, non-hedged yes/no with reasoning. Phase 2 must be an enumerated list of at least four distinct objections, framed adversarially, with no rebuttals embedded. Phase 3 must address each Phase-2 objection individually (revise-or-rebut) and end with an explicit final recommendation, plus an explicit statement of whether/what moved from Phase 1.
evals.tone: Senior staff engineer / technical-advisor voice: direct, decisive, willing to disagree with leadership and defend the disagreement on the merits. Adversarial and unsparing in Phase 2; measured and intellectually honest in Phase 3 (concedes real ground without capitulating). Not academic, not waffly.

evals.expected: The single correct value is 6, output as the bare integer `6` and nothing else. A /29 leaves 32 − 29 = 3 host bits → 2^3 = 8 total addresses; subtracting the network address and the broadcast address yields 8 − 2 = 6 USABLE host addresses. The word "usable" is load-bearing: it is the trap. A strong direct-answer execution returns exactly `6`. Failure modes a judge must catch: (1) Confident wrong answer — returning `8` (forgot to subtract network+broadcast) or `7` (subtracted only one) is the dominant near-miss and should be scored low on accuracy; both are plausible bare values with no trace, exactly the risk this pattern amplifies. (2) Format mismatch — any output other than the bare digit fails format compliance: "6 hosts", "6.", "Six", "6 usable addresses", a leading/trailing space, a sentence, or a code fence. (3) Preamble leakage — any acknowledgment, restatement, "The answer is", or trailing caveat ("though this assumes...") violates the no-preamble/no-explanation constraint even if `6` appears somewhere inside. (4) Silent over-hedging — refusing to commit, offering a range ("6-8 depending on configuration"), or appending the arithmetic is a direct-answer failure. The ONLY fully-correct output is the two characters that form the integer 6 with no whitespace, no punctuation, no other tokens.

evals.expected: A strong reply does ALL of the following. (1) Leads with attunement, NOT a plan: it names the specific, real emotions present — the collision of a hard-won opportunity with a sick parent, the paralysis/freezing, and especially the shame ("I feel pathetic") — and gently reframes the shame (freezing in the face of an impossible choice is a normal human response to a genuine dilemma, not a defect). (2) Uses CONCRETE, specific language tied to THIS situation ("being pulled between Denver and your mom," "a Friday deadline pressing on a decision that deserves more than a week") rather than abstract affirmations ("your feelings are valid," "that sounds really hard"). Generic scripted validation is the primary failure to penalize. (3) Calibrates register correctly: this is a serious adult dilemma, not a catastrophe — over-soft, grief-counselor cooing or pet-name warmth reads as patronizing and should be penalized; so should clinical detachment. (4) Crucially, does NOT collapse into pure witnessing that ignores the real Friday deadline (validation-in-place-of-help / avoidance-enablement): the person freezes and avoids, so an ideal reply, AFTER acknowledging feelings, gently keeps the door to the decision open — e.g., offering presence ("I'm here if you want to talk it through, or just vent") or naming that the deadline is real without pushing — WITHOUT dumping a pros/cons framework, a decision matrix, or telling them what to do (they did not ask for solutions). (5) Honors "don't jump to solutions unless they ask": no unsolicited advice, no "have you considered," no listing options. The hardest needle to thread, and the main discriminator, is #2+#4 together: warmth that is concrete and that neither solutionizes nor enables continued avoidance of a deadline-bound choice. A reply that only mirrors feelings back in a loop, amplifying the freeze, is a failure; so is one that pivots into coaching.
evals.format_spec: Free-form prose, no headings, bullets, or numbered lists (structure would clinicalize the reply and conflicts with the pattern). Short — roughly 3 to 6 sentences / one to two short paragraphs; the pattern favors brevity, and a long reply risks reflective-listening loops. First-person, conversational, addressed directly to the coworker ("you"). Emotional acknowledgment must come first, before anything resembling a next step or offer.

evals.expected: A strong turn-1 response asks EXACTLY ONE question and nothing else substantive — no fix, no SQL, no stacked follow-ups. The single question must be the highest-leverage diagnostic for a slow Postgres query: the canonical best opener is a request for the actual query text together with its EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) plan (or, acceptably, "what is the query and can you share its EXPLAIN ANALYZE output") — because without the query + plan no meaningful diagnosis is possible, so it dominates table size, indexes, pg_stat data, row estimates, etc. Asking instead about schema/table size/index list/Postgres version FIRST is a weaker (off-target-ordering) choice that should cost Accuracy, since those are downstream of seeing the plan. The response must NOT: (a) ask multiple questions at once / present a checklist or numbered battery of questions (question-stacking failure mode); (b) declare "I have enough to proceed" or output an optimization plan now (premature-exit failure mode — it has zero information); (c) restate the whole template back or pad with a long preamble (efficiency). A brief one-line role acknowledgment before the single question is acceptable and arguably good for tone, but it must not become a lecture. The question should be specific and actionable (tells the user exactly what to paste, e.g. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output), not vague ("tell me about your query"). Bonus quality signals: explaining in one short clause WHY this is the first question, and signalling that more questions will follow.
evals.format_spec: Conversational single-turn output containing exactly ONE question. No SQL, no optimization plan, no "I have enough to proceed" signal at this stage. Optional one-line role/intent acknowledgment is permitted; a numbered or bulleted list of multiple questions is a format violation. The question should be plain prose (optionally one short clarifying sub-clause), not a multi-item form.
evals.tone: Professional, consultative, concise — a senior consultant conducting a focused diagnostic intake; warm enough to keep the user engaged but not chatty or padded.

evals.expected:
A single valid JSON object, no surrounding prose, with exactly the five keys IN THE SPECIFIED ORDER. Substantive correctness, tied to the pattern's failure modes (the transcript is engineered so a model that "summarizes the middle" instead of obeying the anchors fails):
- root_cause must identify the VENDOR auth config push at 02:04 as the trigger (msg [02:36]/[02:04]), ending in a [HH:MM] timestamp. It must NOT name deploy 19c (an explicitly-retracted red herring at [02:31]) nor the DB pool (explicitly labeled a secondary symptom, not a cause, at [02:33]/[02:48]).
- LAST-value rule (instruction 4, the lost-in-the-middle trap): any latency figure cited must use the resolved/last value, not the first-mentioned 4200ms or 3800ms. The stable checkout p99 is 780ms [02:46]; if a "before" figure is referenced it should be the corrected 3800/3700ms, never the retracted 4200ms spike. The DB pool, if mentioned, must use 198/300 (corrected at [02:17]), never the misleading "198/200 saturated" first claim [02:15].
- contributing_factors: EXACTLY 2, each one sentence ending in [HH:MM]. The two defensible ones are (a) the no-jitter 3-retry storm amplifying load [02:39], and (b) the brief DB pool exhaustion at 300/300 for ~40s as a secondary effect [02:33]. A flawed answer lists 3+, or includes deploy 19c, or drops the [HH:MM].
- ranked_remediations: EXACTLY 3, ordered by impact. Strong answers lead with fixing the retry policy (add jitter / exponential backoff / circuit-breaker on the payments upstream) since that is the one in-house amplifier, then vendor escalation/failover, then retry-storm protection for the DB pool. Order should be defensible, not arbitrary.
- confidence: should be "high" or "medium" — NOT "low", because instruction 6 gates "low" on an UNRESOLVED trigger contradiction, and the trigger IS resolved (vendor confirms at [02:36], deploy ruled out at [02:31]). Choosing "low" is a misread of the conditional anchor.
- Redaction (instruction 5): ZERO occurrences of Priya, Marcus, Lena, Tom, Dana; no @-handles, no INC-48817/INC-48819, no priya@shopco.io / escalations@payvendor.com, no 10.4.22.7. People referenced by role only (oncall engineer, SRE, DBA, vendor liaison, manager). Any leaked PII/ID/IP is a hard accuracy+safety failure — the [02:11], [02:26], and [02:49] lines are deliberate bait.
- incident_window should be derived (≈02:11 detection to 02:46 stable, or 02:05/02:04 onset to 02:46), expressed sensibly.
A perfect answer satisfies every count, ends every required sentence in a valid [HH:MM], leaks nothing redactable, applies the last-value rule, and sets confidence high/medium.

Exactly five top-level keys in this exact order: "incident_window", "root_cause", "contributing_factors", "ranked_remediations", "confidence". "root_cause" is a string; "contributing_factors" is an array of exactly 2 strings; "ranked_remediations" is an array of exactly 3 strings (most-impactful first); "confidence" is one of "high"|"medium"|"low". Every string in root_cause and contributing_factors must end with a [HH:MM] timestamp token. No human names, @-handles, ticket IDs, email addresses, or IP addresses anywhere in the output.
evals.tone: Terse, factual, machine-consumable incident-postmortem register for an SRE/on-call audience; no conversational framing, no hedging prose outside the JSON.

evals.expected: A strong answer threads numeric results through a correctly ORDERED chain and ends feasible. Required chain and numbers: (1) Raw handle-time workload = 9,600 contacts x 7.5 min = 72,000 min = 1,200 agent-hours/week (and per day: weekday 1,600 x 7.5 = 12,000 min = 200 hrs; weekend 800 x 7.5 = 6,000 min = 100 hrs). (2) Apply the 120% service multiplier to handle-time hours: 1,200 x 1.20 = 1,440 productive hours/week; weekday 200 x 1.2 = 240 hrs/day, weekend 100 x 1.2 = 120 hrs/day. (3) Gross up for 80% productive availability (divide by 0.8): 1,440 / 0.8 = 1,800 PAID agent-hours/week; weekday 240/0.8 = 300 paid hrs/day, weekend 120/0.8 = 150 paid hrs/day. The 120% and the 0.8 gross-up MUST both be applied and in the right place (multiplier on workload, divide by availability) - omitting either, or multiplying by 0.8 instead of dividing, is the key accuracy failure. (4) Split each day into two EQUAL shifts: weekday = 150 paid hrs/shift, weekend = 75 paid hrs/shift. (5) Convert per-shift hours to integer agents per shift at 8 paid hrs/shift, rounding UP (cannot staff a fraction): weekday 150/8 = 18.75 -> 19 agents/shift; weekend 75/8 = 9.375 -> 10 agents/shift. Per-shift-per-day table should show 19 (weekday morning), 19 (weekday evening), 10 (weekend morning), 10 (weekend evening). (6) Weekly shift-demand count = sum of agents x shifts = weekdays (5 days x 2 shifts x 19 = 190 shift-slots) + weekends (2 days x 2 shifts x 10 = 40 shift-slots) = 230 agent-shifts demanded. (7) Each agent supplies 5 shifts/week, so a lower bound on headcount = ceil(230 / 5) = 46 agents. (8) Feasibility / hardest step: the no-same-day-both-shifts rule means an agent can cover at most ONE of the two shifts on any given day; this caps an agent at 5 shifts across 5 distinct days and means each shift-slot needs a distinct agent on that day, but daily peak demand (19+19 = 38 distinct agents needed on a weekday, since morning and evening agents must be different people) is the binding constraint, not just the 230/5 average. A rigorous answer checks the peak: a weekday needs 38 distinct agents present that day; with 46 agents this is satisfiable, and 46 agents x 5 shifts = 230 capacity exactly matches 230 demand, so utilization is 100% and the schedule is tight but achievable IF the 38-distinct-per-weekday and one-shift-per-agent-per-day constraints can be simultaneously met. The strongest answers note that 46 is feasible only because 230 demand = 230 supply exactly and explicitly reconcile the average bound (46) against the daily-distinct-agent peak (38 < 46, so peak is not binding) - concluding YES, 46 agents, schedule achievable. An answer that reports 46 without the feasibility reconciliation, or that mishandles the both-shifts rule, is incomplete. Common wrong finals: forgetting round-up (gives ~45), skipping the 0.8 gross-up (gives ~37), or applying 0.8 as a multiplier instead of divisor.
evals.format_spec: Two explicitly labeled phases. Phase 1 is an ORDERED numbered list of sub-problems (easiest first), each annotating which prior sub-problem's result it consumes. Phase 2 solves them in that same order, and for each step after the first restates the carried-forward numeric input(s) before using them. Must include a per-shift-per-day staffing table (weekday morning/evening, weekend morning/evening) and a single clearly stated final answer (total agents + feasibility yes/no).
evals.tone: Precise, quantitative workforce-planning / operations-analyst voice; numerically explicit and auditable; no hand-waving.

evals.expected: A strong banner is 55-60 words (uses the budget without overshooting it; overshoot past ~66 words = the documented "budget overshoot" failure, and a thin 25-35 word banner that drops actionable facts = "budget underuse"). Within that cap it must triage to the highest-value, action-enabling facts and include ALL of: (1) WHAT is broken — charge creation / POST /v1/charges failing intermittently (~40% / 503s); (2) the safe action the integrator can take NOW — retry with the same Idempotency-Key, called out as safe / no double-charge risk (this is the single most decision-relevant fact and omitting it is the textbook "critical-content omission"); (3) when the next update lands (by 15:00 UTC). It should ideally also signal scope-reassurance compactly — that refunds/payouts/dashboard are unaffected and/or it is a partial degradation not a full outage — but a strong answer may justifiably compress or drop the lower-priority items (exact start time, "rollback in progress", the eu-central-1 regional carve-out) to protect the budget, which is exactly the explicit-prioritization behavior the prompt demands. evals.expected: A strong answer is exactly 8 lines, each `N. <answer>`, with zero preamble/caveats/reasoning, AND is correct on the trap items where terse mode tempts the common-but-wrong reply. evals.expected: A strong answer has two parts. PART 1 (acknowledgement): restates all five bindings accurately and distinctly, NOT collapsing the near-synonyms — `>>safety` (safety-only, tagged bullets) must be kept distinct from `>>review` (full review, prose), and `>>safe?` (one-word YES/NO) distinct from `>>safety`; it then explicitly WAITS and does not review the migration yet (acting prematurely is a fail). PART 2 (applying the chained follow-up), which must honor each invoked token in order and in its specified format: (a) `>>safety` — safety-only bullets, each tagged [BLOCKER]/[WARN], correctly identifying the real Postgres hazards: ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL DEFAULT is actually SAFE on modern PG 11+ (a sophisticated answer notes this rather than flagging it as a blocker — flagging it is a substantive accuracy error), ALTER COLUMN total TYPE numeric forces a full table rewrite + ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock [BLOCKER], CREATE INDEX (non-CONCURRENTLY) takes a lock blocking writes [BLOCKER/WARN], and ADD CONSTRAINT FOREIGN KEY without NOT VALID takes a lock and scans/validates all rows [BLOCKER/WARN]; no style/naming comments; (b) `>>split` — a numbered, ordered, separately-deployable sequence that fixes those hazards (e.g. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a later step, a batched/backfill strategy for the type change); (c) `>>safe?` — a single line, just NO (it is not safe as written), no explanation. A strong answer must FLAG that `>>downgrade` is unbound and ask/decline rather than silently guessing it means rollback — and must NOT emit a down-migration unprompted. Honoring `>>rollback` here despite it not being typed, or producing reverse SQL, is the over-extension failure mode.

Phase 1: an acknowledgement that lists/restates all five bindings and an explicit statement that it is waiting for the first instruction (no migration analysis yet). evals.expected:
A strong answer is an honest, ordered, gap-free migration runbook that survives all five recipe-pattern failure modes:

PREREQUISITES (step-skipping test — a weak answer jumps straight to ALTER): must list, before any schema change, (a) verify a recent backup / PITR is available and confirm restore path, (b) measure current max(id) and headroom vs int4 ceiling (2,147,483,647) to size urgency, (c) check replica lag and disk headroom (the migration roughly doubles space for the new column + indexes), (d) audit ALL referencing FKs — the three child tables' FK columns are ALSO int4 and must be migrated too (a recipe that re-types only orders.id and forgets the FK columns is silently broken).

CORE TECHNIQUE (accuracy test): must reject the naive single-statement `ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN id TYPE bigint` — on 900M rows this rewrites the whole table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and blocks all reads/writes for a long time, violating zero-downtime. The correct shape is the additive/backfill/swap dance: (1) add a new nullable `id_bigint bigint` column (fast, metadata-only in PG11+; adding WITH a non-null default would rewrite — flag), (2) backfill in batches with throttling/commit-per-batch to avoid long transactions and replica lag, (3) keep new column in sync for new/updated rows via trigger OR application dual-write, (4) add a UNIQUE index CONCURRENTLY on id_bigint, plus the same additive treatment on each child FK column, (5) build new FK constraints as NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (validate takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, not a full lock), (6) the swap: inside a short transaction take a brief lock to drop old PK/FKs and rename columns / promote id_bigint to PK, sequencing parent and children correctly. Must also address the sequence: the identity/serial sequence still emits int4-range values unless re-pointed / recreated as bigint, and Rails schema (schema.rb / structure.sql + model) must be reconciled or the next deploy fights the DB.

REVERSIBILITY FLAGS (the load-bearing test): must explicitly flag as irreversible / point-of-no-return: dropping the old `id` column (data loss — cannot un-drop), dropping/replacing the old PK and FK constraints, the rename/swap transaction, decommissioning the backfill trigger or stopping dual-write before validation, and ANY DROP/destructive sequence change. A mediocre answer buries the DROP COLUMN in the numbered list with no warning — that is the documented failure this prompt is built to expose. Should advise keeping the old column for a cooldown period before the final drop, and a verification step (counts/checksums match) gating the drop.

ENVIRONMENT FIT (portability test): must respect the stated constraints — no maintenance window (so no plain ALTER, no `VACUUM FULL`), no superuser/filesystem access (so no `pg_repack` requiring extension install unless noted as needing provider support, no logical-replication tricks needing superuser), rolling Rails deploys (so the dual-write/trigger must be live before and during backfill and the cutover must tolerate mixed old/new app code — strong answers order the Rails deploy steps to interleave safely with the DB steps). A recipe assuming a window, superuser, or pg_repack-by-default fails environment-fit.

FOLLOW-UP / CLEANUP (completeness test): re-VALIDATE FKs, ANALYZE/refresh stats, drop the sync trigger after cutover, drop old column after cooldown, fix the sequence ownership, update Rails schema dump + remove dual-write code in a later deploy, and monitor replica lag and bloat throughout.

A 5/5 nails the additive/backfill/concurrent-index/NOT-VALID-then-VALIDATE technique AND the child-FK columns AND flags every destructive step AND fits the no-window/no-superuser environment. Typical mid-tier flaws that should pull the score into the 2.5-4.5 band: forgetting the three child FK columns, proposing a plain ALTER COLUMN TYPE (or pg_repack) that breaks zero-downtime, omitting CONCURRENTLY / NOT VALID, missing the sequence re-type, or listing DROP COLUMN with no irreversibility flag.
evals.format_spec: A single numbered, ordered recipe covering prerequisite, core, and follow-up/cleanup steps as one continuous sequence (sections allowed, but steps globally ordered and executable top-to-bottom). Each step must carry its required inputs/tools and the concrete command or SQL. Irreversible/expensive-to-reverse steps must be explicitly and visibly flagged (e.g. a warning marker or label), not merely embedded in prose. The artifact must be self-contained / portable — no "consult your DBA" hand-waving in place of an actual step.
evals.tone: Operational runbook tone for a competent senior backend/SRE engineer: precise, imperative, technical, no hedging filler. Assumes SQL and Rails fluency; explains a choice only where the choice is dangerous or non-obvious.

evals.expected:
A strong answer is judged primarily on whether Phase 2 surfaces the REAL, substantive gaps a first-draft rollback runbook predictably has, and whether Phase 3 actually closes them (not rewords).

DRAFT (Phase 1): A plausible but imperfect rollback procedure — reverting app code (redeploy previous image/tag or git revert), and some handling of the migration. It will almost certainly under-specify the hard part: a code rollback alone does NOT undo the schema change, and the migration as described is partially destructive (it dropped an old column), so a naive "just run the down-migration" is unsafe.

CRITIQUE (Phase 2) — a STRONG critique must name concrete, technically-correct defects, the kind below (at least 3, each pointing to a specific part of the draft):
- The dropped column is unrecoverable by a down-migration — reverting the schema cannot restore data already lost when the old column was dropped; the draft likely ignores this and must flag it (fix: confirm whether reverting code even requires the schema revert, or whether the safer path is roll-forward, since the migration was destructive).
- Code/schema coupling ordering: if you revert app code first while the new schema is still live, or revert schema while new code is live, you can deepen the outage; the draft likely doesn't specify the safe order (revert app code to a version compatible with the CURRENT schema, OR confirm old code tolerates the new column, before touching the DB).
- Backward compatibility of the OLD code with the NEW schema (the added NOT NULL column / dropped old column) — old app code may break against the changed schema, so a blind code rollback may not be safe; must be checked.
- No verification / success criteria — how the on-call confirms the rollback worked (500 rate returns to baseline, healthcheck, monitoring/dashboard, error budget).
- Missing safeguards: take a backup/snapshot before any destructive DB action, announce/declare the incident + comms, lock the pipeline to prevent a re-deploy racing the rollback, transaction/locking risk of the backfill on a large table.
- Migration tooling specifics: whether a down/rollback migration exists and is tested, and that running it is itself risky.

REVISION (Phase 3) — a STRONG revision must INCORPORATE the fixes named in Phase 2 with new substantive content: explicit safe ordering of code-vs-schema steps, an explicit statement that the dropped column's data is gone and the resulting decision (prefer roll-forward / fix-forward when the migration is destructive, or restore-from-backup if data loss is unacceptable), a pre-rollback snapshot step, verification/success criteria, and incident comms / pipeline freeze. It must be numbered/sequential, runnable under pressure, and ~300-450 words.

FLAWS A JUDGE SHOULD PENALIZE (tied to the pattern's failure modes):
- Self-flattery: Phase 2 lists only cosmetic nits (formatting, tone) and misses the destructive-migration / ordering problem — the single most important real defect. This is the most likely and most detectable failure.
- Vague critique: "could add more detail about the database" with no concrete defect named.
- Cosmetic revision: Phase 3 reorders headings or rewords but does NOT add the destructive-column handling, safe ordering, snapshot, or verification that Phase 2 (if good) identified.
- Critique-revision mismatch: Phase 3 fixes things not raised in Phase 2 (e.g., adds emojis) while ignoring a gap Phase 2 explicitly named.
- Regression: Phase 3 introduces a new unsafe instruction (e.g., "run the down-migration immediately") while polishing prose, or blows past the word budget.
A top answer's revision is materially safer and more complete than its draft, and every Phase-2 item maps to a visible Phase-3 change.
evals.format_spec: Exactly three labeled phases in order: "Phase 1 - Draft", "Phase 2 - Critique", "Phase 3 - Revision" (phase labels must be present and distinct; phases must not be merged). Phase 2 must be a list of 3 to 5 items, each naming a concrete defect AND its fix. Phase 3 must be a standalone, self-contained rewrite (no "as above" / back-references), formatted as a numbered/sequential procedure, and roughly 300-450 words.
evals.tone: Operational/technical, calm and directive — runbook prose an on-call engineer can execute under pressure (imperative steps, no hedging). The critique phase is candid and self-critical, not self-congratulatory.

It must confirm eligibility was checked (74>=60) rather than silently skipped. It must NOT 'correct' the x1.25 multiplier, the inclusive day counts, or the $1,500 flat clawback into something else (the verification-introduces-error trap): e.g. wrongly re-prorating the clawback, applying the multiplier after the cap, treating the cap as a floor, or recomputing 9,758.24 as a 'cleaner' wrong number. If the first pass already had 9,500 correct, the strong move is a substantive confirmation that re-derives the numbers and explicitly clears each constraint, NOT a one-line 'looks correct.' If the first pass erred (e.g. 73 days -> different proration, or wrong cap/clawback order), the verification pass MUST catch and fix it to 9,500. Subtle-flaw detectors for the judge: (1) final != 9,500; (2) day count != 74 unfixed; (3) eligibility gate never mentioned; (4) cap/clawback order asserted wrongly with no recognition; (5) clawback prorated or capped-after; (6) verification that merely restates the first pass without independent re-derivation (rubber-stamp); (7) verification that flips a correct step to an incorrect one.
evals.format_spec: Two clearly delimited passes. Pass 1: a step-by-step worked solution with each labeled stage shown (days engaged, eligibility check, prorated base, multiplier, cap, clawback, final figure) and a stated final bonus. Pass 2: an explicit review/audit section that re-derives the day count and arithmetic independently and checks each named constraint (eligibility threshold, cap-vs-clawback order, non-negative floor), then states either 'no errors found' with the confirmed figure or the specific corrections and a single revised final bonus figure. The final bonus must appear as one unambiguous dollar amount.
evals.tone: Precise, methodical, auditor-like; numerate and explicit about each step. Plain professional register, no flourish; suitable for a finance/ops reviewer who will trust the number.

evals.expected: A strong answer commits to ONE recommendation (the technically defensible one is: split the two tables' problems — option (a)'s replica+cache solves the read-heavy `accounts` hot path cheaply and first, while the write-heavy append-only `events` table points toward option (c)'s columnar/time-series store, with sharding (b) explicitly deprioritized as premature operational complexity for a 9-person team). It must respect BOTH phases distinctly. Phase 1 must be 3-7 genuine HEADINGS, each 3-10 words, with NO reasoning, justification, or conclusions embedded (e.g. "Recommended path and rationale", "Sequencing across the two quarters", "What we trade away", "Failure modes and mitigations", "Decision triggers / what would change this") — a skeleton whose bullets already contain the recommendation or its reasons is the skeleton-as-answer / phase-bleed failure. Phase 2 must expand each heading IN THE SAME ORDER, and each expansion must actually address its own heading (no drift: the "trade-offs" section must discuss trade-offs, not re-argue the recommendation — expansion-mismatch failure). Critically, depth must be NON-UNIFORM: the recommendation+rationale and the failure-modes sections are load-bearing and deserve the full 4 sentences with specifics (replica lag and read-after-write/staleness on `accounts`, cache invalidation strategy, dual-write/backfill risk and eventual-consistency for the `events` columnar move, the cost of NOT sharding), while a section like "what would change this" can be legitimately shorter — an answer that gives all 5 points identical canned depth is the over-uniform-expansion failure and should be marked down. Substantive correctness markers: addresses read-after-write consistency for replicas, names a concrete cache-invalidation approach for `accounts`, recognizes append-only `events` as a poor sharding/relational fit and good columnar fit, sequences cheap-and-reversible work (replica+cache) before expensive-and-sticky work (data-store migration), and names real failure modes (replica lag, cache stampede/staleness, dual-write divergence during migration) rather than generic ones.
evals.format_spec: Two clearly labeled phases. Phase 1 ("Phase 1: Skeleton") is a numbered list of 3-7 bullets, each 3-10 words, with no elaboration. Phase 2 ("Phase 2: Expansion") repeats those numbered headings in identical order, each followed by a 2-4 sentence prose expansion. No content in Phase 1 beyond the headings; no new headings introduced in Phase 2 that were absent from the skeleton.
evals.tone: Pragmatic senior-engineer / staff-level decision memo addressed to a small engineering team and their lead; opinionated and concrete, not hedging or survey-style; assumes technical fluency.

evals.expected: A strong answer makes all four stages visibly distinct AND substantively different (defeating the 'conservative passes' failure mode). Concrete markers a judge can check: STAGE DISCIPLINE — Stage 2 confines itself to factual/logical fixes and carries a real, non-empty "Corrections:" note; idempotency has well-known traps a correct draft is unlikely to nail on the first try, so a credible answer surfaces at least one genuine correction (e.g. it initially said the SERVER generates the key, or that a key collision should silently return the cached response regardless of body, or conflated idempotency with caching/locking, or claimed POST is idempotent by HTTP spec — and fixes it). "Corrections: none" is only acceptable if Stage 1 was already fully correct, which is a high bar; an empty note paired with a Stage 1 that DID contain an error is a detectable stage-bleed/skipping flaw. NO STAGE BLEED — Stage 3 must not introduce new technical claims or fix correctness silently (if a fact first appears or changes in Stage 3, that's a flaw); Stage 4 must not repair correctness or clarity. CONTENT COMPLETENESS preserved to the end — all six required points (a–f) must survive into Stage 4: definition + the double-charge-on-retry failure; client-generated key reused across retries (server must NOT generate it); server stores key→response and returns the SAME stored response (typically with no re-execution) on a duplicate; same-key-different-body must be REJECTED (e.g. 409/422), never served the stale response; a stated retention window (e.g. 24h–7d) with the reasoning that keys expire and must not be reused for new logical requests; and the pitfall (e.g. persisting/caching the response before the downstream charge is confirmed, risking returning success for a charge that failed). REGRESSION CHECK — the Stage 4 concision pass is where weak models drop point (d), (e), or (f) to hit the word target; a strong answer hits ~30% reduction (Stage 4 roughly 0.65–0.75× Stage 3 words) while ALL six points remain, and reports an accurate "Word count: N". CORRECTNESS TECHNICAL BAR — must not claim POST is natively idempotent, must not say the server generates the key, must not treat same-key-different-body as a cache hit, and must locate response-caching AFTER downstream success.
evals.format_spec: Four explicitly labeled stage outputs in order (Stage 1, Stage 2, Stage 3, Stage 4). Stage 2 must open with a "Corrections:" line. Stage 4 must end with a "Word count: N" line and represent roughly a 30% word reduction versus Stage 3. The final deliverable is the Stage 4 text. No invented extra stages, no merged/split stages.
evals.tone: Clear, precise internal engineering-documentation voice for backend engineers who know HTTP but are new to idempotency; instructive and matter-of-fact, not marketing-flavored.

evals.expected: A strong answer (1) names the correct governing principle up front: decisions should compare only future/differential cash flows — sunk costs are irrelevant and the still-owed $150,000 loan is irrelevant because it is incurred identically under both options (it is not a sunk cost in the historical sense but is a non-differential common cost, and opportunity cost / salvage must be counted). It must explicitly flag that the $240k purchase, the $90k payments, and the $60k already spent are SUNK and must be excluded — resisting the bait to "recoup the investment." (2) It then derives the answer using ONLY differential future costs. Correct computation: KEEP = 3 × $58,000 = $174,000 in operating cost; it must also count the FORGONE $40,000 resale (opportunity cost of keeping) — so KEEP effective cost = $174,000 + $40,000 = $214,000. REPLACE = $180,000 purchase − $40,000 from selling the old press − $50,000 salvage at year 3 + (3 × $22,000 = $66,000) operating = $180,000 − $40,000 − $50,000 + $66,000 = $156,000. The $150,000 loan balance is common to both and correctly drops out (or, if included on both sides, nets to zero). REPLACE is cheaper by $214,000 − $156,000 = $58,000. Recommendation: replace. A correct answer need not present the $40k as an opportunity cost on KEEP (it may instead subtract it from REPLACE and not add it to KEEP); either symmetric treatment yields the same $58,000 gap, and the strong answer keeps the treatment consistent across both options. Subtle flaws a judge should catch: including any sunk figure ($240k/$90k/$60k) in the comparison (wrong-abstraction: "total cost of ownership" / "recoup the investment"); including the $150k loan on only one side; double-counting or omitting the $40k resale or the $50k salvage; stating the marginal-cost principle in the preamble but then computing with sunk or loan figures anyway (abstraction theater); or retreating to a vacuous principle ("this is a cost-benefit / business decision") that doesn't name sunk-cost irrelevance and opportunity cost. A wrong but confident answer that "keeps the press to avoid wasting the $240k already invested" is the canonical wrong-abstraction failure and must score low on accuracy.
evals.format_spec: Two clearly separated parts: (1) a stated broader principle in 1-3 sentences placed BEFORE the worked answer, and (2) a derivation that uses that principle, showing the side-by-side cost comparison (the two totals), the numeric difference, and an explicit recommendation. The principle must precede and visibly drive the math, not appear as a post-hoc label.
evals.tone: Practical, advisory, numerate — a finance/operations analyst advising a small-business owner; plain language, no jargon dumps, but rigorous about what counts and what doesn't.

evals.expected: A single, parseable JSON object (parses cleanly with a strict parser on the first try) with no surrounding prose and no ```/```json fences. Field-by-field, a strong answer MUST have: ticket_id "A-2291" (the TICKET# prefix stripped, or at most "A-2291"; "TICKET#A-2291" is acceptable but the bare ID is cleaner); customer_email "o'neil+billing@acme.co" (the apostrophe and + preserved verbatim — JSON does not require escaping a single quote, and a model that backslash-escapes it produces invalid/incorrect content); severity "critical" (SEV-1 / urgent maps to the top tier — mapping it to "high" or leaving "SEV-1" is the silent-failure trap); product_versions exactly ["3.10.0-rc2","3.9.4"] as an array of two strings; error_message preserving the verbatim text including the internal double quotes around } and the backslashes in C:\app\config.json:42 — this is the crux: the embedded " characters MUST be escaped as \" and each backslash as \\ so the string is valid JSON yet decodes back to the original literal text (failing to escape = malformed JSON; over-escaping or dropping characters = wrong content); minutes_to_first_response MUST be null (the source says "still waiting" / "~" with no value — fabricating a number like 0 is the do-not-guess violation); tags ["parser","regression","windows-only"]; resolved false (status: open). The single most discriminating points are correct backslash+quote escaping inside error_message (valid JSON AND faithful content simultaneously) and emitting null rather than a fabricated 0 for the missing response time.
evals.format_spec: Exactly one JSON object and nothing else: no preamble, no trailing text, no markdown code fences. Must parse with a strict JSON parser on the first attempt (no trailing commas, no comments, all strings double-quoted, embedded double-quotes escaped as \" and backslashes as \\). All eight keys present in the schema's order; product_versions and tags are JSON arrays; minutes_to_first_response is a JSON number or null; resolved is a JSON boolean.
evals.tone: Machine-facing, zero-prose classifier/extractor output destined directly for a parser; no human-readable commentary whatsoever.

evals.expected: A STRONG answer is exactly one parseable JSON object, no prose/fences, with every schema field present and correctly typed. Field-level reference: incident_id MUST be null (the narrative names no official ID — fabricating one like "INC-001" is the empty-slot failure mode). severity = "SEV1" (the FINAL/confirmed severity after the IC bumped it; "SEV2" is the initial value and is wrong — tests reading "final/confirmed" correctly). root_cause_category = "configuration" (the config push is the proximate cause; "deployment"/"human-error" are tempting distractors the narrative dangles — "the deploy pipeline should have caught it" — but the category asks for root cause, which was the config change). detection_source = "customer-report" (a customer tweet flagged by support came FIRST, before the automated alert; choosing "automated-alert" misreads the corrected ordering). time_to_detect_minutes: best answer is 15 (impact 14:05 → detection/declared at alert 14:20); accepting null with a justification is defensible given the explicitly hedged/contradictory timestamps, but a fabricated false-precision number that ignores the stated conflict is weak. time_to_resolve_minutes = 90 (14:05 → 15:35). customer_impacting = true (boolean true, not the string "true"). affected_services = exactly ["payments-api","order-service","checkout"] (the web/checkout flow counts; the internal admin dashboard MUST be excluded — it was explicitly fine). action_items = an array of two objects: {pre-deploy/pool config validation, owner "Priya", due ~"2026-06-26"/"2026-06-27" i.e. end of next week relative to 2026-06-20, or null if the model declines to resolve "end of next week"} and {faster latency alert, owner null, due null}. data_loss = false (boolean). notes MUST capture the unschematized material fact that this is the second time this quarter the replica-routing config caused an incident — this is the over-constraint escape hatch; dropping it entirely is the over-constraint failure mode, and stuffing it into a wrong field is also wrong. A flawed-but-plausible answer will typically (a) pick SEV2 or "deployment"/"human-error", (b) pick automated-alert, (c) fabricate incident_id, (d) include the admin dashboard, (e) drop the recurrence fact from notes, or (f) emit booleans/integers as strings.
evals.format_spec: A single valid JSON object and nothing else — no markdown code fences, no leading/trailing prose. Must contain exactly the schema's keys (no invented top-level fields, no omitted fields). Enum fields must use one of the listed literal values. customer_impacting and data_loss must be JSON booleans (true/false), not strings. time_to_detect_minutes / time_to_resolve_minutes must be JSON integers or null, not strings. affected_services is an array of strings. action_items is an array of objects each with description/owner/due keys. evals.tone: Machine-consumable extraction output for a downstream incident-database ingest pipeline; no human-facing narration, no hedging prose, no apologies — the JSON is the entire deliverable.

(or "platform") to confirm reversibility / coordinate the schema rollback — the correct use of page_human's when_to_use (knowledge/authorization the agent lacks), NOT as a lazy first move.
